name: Chapter 13: Plant Growth and Development
description: Growth phases and rates, differentiation, plasticity, and the five plant growth regulators

cards.term: Development is the sum of which two processes?
cards.definition: Growth and differentiation
Seed germination

cards.term: What happens to seeds when conditions are unfavourable?
cards.definition: They do not germinate and enter a period of suspended growth or rest

cards.term: Figure 13.1 · Germination and seedling development in bean
Bean germination: which part forms a hook, and why?
cards.definition: The epicotyl hook (NCERT fig.) protects the delicate shoot tip as it pushes through soil. Bean shows epigeal-type emergence of the cotyledons above the soil line.
An irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or an individual cell
Yes: both anabolic and catabolic processes, at the expense of energy

cards.term: Is a piece of wood swelling in water growth?
cards.definition: No. It is reversible imbibition, not a permanent increase with metabolism.

cards.term: Why is plant growth called indeterminate?
cards.definition: Plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life, due to meristems

cards.term: What is the open form of growth?
cards.definition: New cells are always being added to the plant body by meristem activity
Root and shoot apical meristems: elongation along the axis

cards.term: Which meristems cause secondary growth, and in which plants?
cards.definition: Vascular cambium and cork cambium (lateral meristems): increase in girth, in dicots and gymnosperms

cards.term: Growth at the cellular level is mainly due to?
cards.definition: Increase in the amount of protoplasm
Fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume, cell number

cards.term: Maize root apical meristem produces how many cells per hour?
cards.definition: More than 17,500

cards.term: Watermelon cells may increase in size by up to?
cards.definition: 3,50,000 times

cards.text: Growth is measured as increase in {{c1::length}} for a pollen tube and increase in {{c2::surface area}} for a dorsiventral leaf.

cards.term: Why is no single parameter good enough for growth through a plant's whole life?
cards.definition: Different organs and stages grow differently (cell number, cell size, length, area), so one parameter misses the others

cards.term: Features of cells in the meristematic phase?
cards.definition: Rich in protoplasm, large nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls, abundant plasmodesmata

cards.term: Features of cells in the elongation phase?
cards.definition: Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, new cell wall deposition

cards.term: Features of cells in the maturation phase?
cards.definition: Maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modification

cards.term: How are growth zones detected in a root (Figure 13.3)?
cards.definition: Parallel line technique: equally spaced marks; zones just behind the apex spread apart most (elongation zone)
Increased growth per unit time

cards.term: Arithmetic growth: what happens after mitosis?
cards.definition: Only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates and matures

cards.term: Geometric growth: what happens after mitosis?
cards.definition: Both daughter cells keep dividing
A root elongating at a constant rate; length vs time gives a straight line
L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + rt (r = elongation per unit time)
W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub> e<sup>rt</sup> (r = relative growth rate)

cards.term: What is r in W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ called?
cards.definition: Relative growth rate, a measure of ability to produce new material: the efficiency index

cards.term: Three phases of the sigmoid growth curve?
cards.definition: Lag (slow), log/exponential (rapid), stationary (limited nutrients)
Limited nutrient supply slows growth to a stationary phase

cards.term: Which growth curve is typical of living organisms in nature?
cards.definition: Sigmoid (S-curve)

cards.term: What growth curve would a tree with seasonal activity show?
cards.definition: A series of stacked S-curves: one sigmoid per growing season
Absolute: total growth per unit time. Relative: growth per unit time per unit initial size.

cards.term: Leaves A (5→10 cm²) and B (50→55 cm²) both grew 5 cm². Which has higher relative growth rate?
cards.definition: A: it doubled (100%) while B grew only 10%. Absolute growth is equal.

cards.term: Figure 13.4 (c): embryo development shows which growth patterns?
cards.definition: An early geometric phase (all cells divide) followed by an arithmetic phase
Water, oxygen, nutrients, optimum temperature; light and gravity affect some stages

cards.term: Two roles of water in growth?
cards.definition: Cell enlargement needs water (turgidity helps extension); water is the medium for enzymes
Releases metabolic energy (respiration)
Synthesis of protoplasm and a source of energy
Maturation of cells from meristems and cambium to perform specific functions

cards.term: How does a cell differentiate into a tracheary element?
cards.definition: Loses its protoplasm and develops strong, elastic lignocellulosic secondary walls
Differentiated cells that lost the capacity to divide regain it
Formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma
Cells from dedifferentiated tissue again lose the capacity to divide and mature for specific functions

cards.term: Examples of redifferentiated tissues in a woody dicot?
cards.definition: Secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork (phellem), secondary cortex

cards.term: What is a callus in tissue culture an example of?
cards.definition: Dedifferentiation: parenchyma made to divide in controlled conditions

cards.text: Differentiation → {{c1::dedifferentiation}} (regain division, e.g. cork cambium) → {{c2::redifferentiation}} (mature again, e.g. cork).

cards.term: Why is differentiation in plants called "open"?
cards.definition: Cells from the same meristem have different structures at maturity, decided by their position

cards.term: Example of position deciding a cell's fate?
cards.definition: Cells pushed away from the root apical meristem become root cap; those pushed to the periphery become epidermis
All changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from germination to senescence

cards.term: Figure 13.8 · Development of a plant cell

cards.definition: Ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to environment or life phase, forming different structures
Different leaf shapes on the same plant: an example of plasticity

cards.term: Heterophylly due to life phase: examples?
cards.definition: Cotton, coriander, larkspur: juvenile leaves differ from adult leaves
Buttercup: leaves in air differ from leaves in water

cards.term: Intrinsic vs extrinsic factors controlling development?
cards.definition: Intrinsic: genetic (intracellular) and PGRs (intercellular). Extrinsic: light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition.
Small, simple molecules of diverse chemistry; also called plant growth substances, plant hormones or phytohormones
Auxin (IAA): Indole compound; Cytokinin (kinetin): Adenine derivative (N⁶-furfurylamino purine); Abscisic acid: Carotenoid derivative; Gibberellic acid (GA₃): Terpene; Ethylene: Gas (C₂H₄)

cards.definition: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins
Abscisic acid (ethylene largely too)
Ethylene: but it is largely an inhibitor
Responses to wounds and stresses, dormancy, abscission
No. All five major groups were discovered accidentally.

cards.term: What did Charles and Francis Darwin observe?
cards.definition: Coleoptiles of canary grass bend towards unilateral light (phototropism); the tip is the source of the influence

cards.term: Who isolated auxin, and from what?
cards.definition: F.W. Went, from coleoptile tips of oat seedlings
"Foolish seedling" disease of rice, caused by the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi: seedlings grow abnormally tall

cards.term: Who linked bakanae to a fungal substance, and when?
cards.definition: E. Kurosawa (1926): sterile fungal filtrates caused the symptoms; the substance was gibberellic acid

cards.term: What did Skoog observe with tobacco callus?
cards.definition: Callus from internode segments grew only if, besides auxin, the medium had vascular extract, yeast extract, coconut milk or DNA
Miller et al. (1955)

cards.term: Three inhibitors later shown to be abscisic acid?
cards.definition: Inhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin (mid-1960s)
H.H. Cousins (1910): ripe oranges released a volatile substance that hastened ripening of stored bananas

Auxin: Darwins (phototropism); Went isolated (oat); Gibberellin: Kurosawa, bakanae of rice; Cytokinin: Skoog; Miller named kinetin; ABA: Inhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin; Ethylene: Cousins, oranges and bananas

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Discovery

Who / what?

AuxinDarwins (phototropism); Went isolated (oat)
GibberellinKurosawa, bakanae of rice
CytokininSkoog; Miller named kinetin
ABAInhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin
EthyleneCousins, oranges and bananas

cards.definition: Greek auxein = to grow

cards.term: From where was auxin first isolated?
cards.definition: Human urine
Growing apices of stems and roots; they migrate to regions of action
Natural: IAA, IBA. Synthetic: NAA, 2,4-D.
Rooting in stem cuttings; flowering in pineapple; prevent early fruit/leaf drop; parthenocarpy in tomato; herbicides; xylem differentiation; cell division
Prevents drop of young leaves and fruits; promotes abscission of older mature ones
The growing apical bud inhibits growth of lateral (axillary) buds

cards.term: What happens on decapitation (removing the shoot tip)?
cards.definition: Lateral buds grow into branches

cards.term: Why are tea bushes and hedges regularly pruned?
cards.definition: Removing apical buds removes apical dominance, so lateral buds branch into a dense bush

cards.term: What is 2,4-D used for, and why is it selective?
cards.definition: Kills dicot weeds but not mature monocots: weed-free lawns and cereal fields

cards.term: Which PGR induces parthenocarpy in tomatoes?
cards.definition: Auxin
More than 100, from fungi and higher plants (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃…)
Gibberellic acid (GA₃)
Acidic
Longer grape stalks; elongate and shape apples; delay senescence; speed malting; increase sugarcane yield; early seeds in conifers; bolting

cards.term: By how much can GA increase sugarcane yield?
cards.definition: Up to 20 tonnes per acre (longer stems store more sugar)

cards.term: What is bolting? Which PGR causes it?
cards.definition: Internode elongation just before flowering in rosette plants (beet, cabbage); caused by gibberellins
GA₃ speeds up the malting process

cards.term: Why do GAs extend the market period of fruits?
cards.definition: They delay senescence, so fruit stays on the tree longer

cards.term: What happens if GA₃ is applied to rice seedlings?
cards.definition: They grow abnormally tall (like bakanae)
Cytokinesis (cell division)
Autoclaved herring sperm DNA

cards.term: Does kinetin occur naturally in plants?
cards.definition: No
Zeatin, from corn kernels and coconut milk
Regions of rapid cell division: root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits
New leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoots; overcome apical dominance; nutrient mobilisation that delays leaf senescence

cards.term: Auxin vs cytokinin on lateral buds?
cards.definition: Auxin (from apex) inhibits them; cytokinin promotes their growth

cards.term: What if you forget cytokinin in tissue culture medium?
cards.definition: Cells will not divide well; callus and shoots will not form

cards.term: Which tissues make large amounts of ethylene?
cards.definition: Tissues undergoing senescence and ripening fruits
Horizontal growth, swelling of the axis, apical hook in dicot seedlings
The rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening, enhanced by ethylene
Respiratory climacteric
Breaks seed and bud dormancy; initiates germination in peanut, sprouting of potato tubers
Rapid internode/petiole elongation keeps upper parts above water
Promotes root growth and root hairs (larger absorption surface)
Initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapple; induces flowering in mango

cards.term: Most widely used source of ethylene?
cards.definition: Ethephon: absorbed in solution, releases ethylene slowly
Hastens ripening of tomatoes, apples; thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut; promotes female flowers in cucumber

cards.term: What happens if a rotten fruit is mixed with unripe fruits?
cards.definition: Its ethylene hastens their ripening

cards.term: Intuition: "one bad apple spoils the barrel"?
cards.definition: Over-ripe fruit releases ethylene, which speeds ripening (and rotting) of neighbours

cards.term: ABA was discovered for which roles?
cards.definition: Regulating abscission and dormancy
General growth and metabolism inhibitor; inhibits germination; closes stomata; increases stress tolerance; seed development, maturation and dormancy

cards.term: Why is ABA called the stress hormone?
cards.definition: It increases tolerance to stresses, e.g. by closing stomata in water stress
Induces dormancy, helping them withstand desiccation

cards.term: ABA is antagonistic to which PGR?
cards.definition: Gibberellins
"ABA says STOP": Stomata close, Dormancy, Abscission (named for it), stress; it Stops germination
Complementary or antagonistic; individualistic or synergistic

cards.term: Events controlled by more than one PGR?
cards.definition: Dormancy, abscission, senescence, apical dominance

cards.term: Which extrinsic factors act through PGRs?
cards.definition: Temperature and light: vernalisation, flowering, dormancy, germination, plant movements

cards.term: Note: exercises mention photoperiodism and vernalisation. Are they in this edition?
cards.definition: Those sections were removed from the current NCERT text; only the exercises remain

Induce rooting in a twig: Auxin (IBA/NAA); Quickly ripen a fruit: Ethylene (ethephon); Delay leaf senescence: Cytokinin; Grow axillary buds: Cytokinin; Bolt a rosette plant: Gibberellin; Close stomata immediately: Abscisic acid
